newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel seen cutting rates nil to 0.3 pct.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel seen cutting rates nil to 0.3 pct.

text.p: Analysts said that the Bank of Israel would either leave interest rates unchanged or else cut them by up to 0.3 percentage points when it announces its March monetary programme on Monday.

The analysts on Sunday said the central bank faces contradictory signals, ranging from a low January consumer price index (CPI) to a widening budget deficit. The daily newspaper Maariv on Sunday said Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel is under pressure from the prime minister's office and the Treasury to make a big cut.

"I think Frenkel is very resistant to this kind of pressure," said Danniella Finn, a vice president at Betucha Securities. "The estimates are for 0.0-0.3 percentage point cut in interest rates....I feel comfortable with those estimates."

The Bank of Israel has cut the base rate 0.5 percentage point in each of the last two months, capping a total reduction of 2.8 points since the middle of last year. The base rate is currently 14.2 percent.
Adam Reuter, managing director of Financial Immunities, a financial consulting firm, predicted Frenkel would lower the rate 0.3 point.

"First they (the Bank of Israel) absorbed the liquidity they injected into the economy, second the CPI was low and finally the state of the economy," he said citing reasons for making a relatively sharp cut.

In a bid to defend the currency basket rate against the Israeli shekel, the Bank of Israel has been routinely intervening in the local currency market since mid-January. But the central bank has said it is successfully absorbing the resulting liquidity.
Although, M1 money supply rose a sharp 3.4 percent in January, analysts have dismissed any connection with the forex market intervention.
Meanwhile, consumer prices rose a moderate 0.4 percent in January, while the economy remains in a slowdown.
Roy Meir, of Simodan brokerage house, said he thought the central bank would hold rates this month.
"The January budget deficit was a lot bigger than expected," he said. "Even though there was a low January consumer price index, that's history. The deficit is still an issue."
He said it was unlikely that rates would come down until the Treasury was able to put spending back on course, which he said would not occur before the end of March.
Reuter said he also doubted rates would continue coming down after this month.
"I think we've reached the end of a trend," he said. "We'll see higher CPIs in March and April because of the strength of the dollar."
